subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Tidal Disruption Events
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Tidal Disruption Events.

hook.text: When a star wanders too close to a black hole, tidal forces rip it apart. The death flare is visible across the cosmos.

buildup.text: The star is stretched and torn into a stream of gas. Some falls in, some is flung away at high speed.

discovery.text: These tidal disruption events produce bright flares in X-ray, ultraviolet, and visible light lasting weeks to months.

twist.text: They reveal dormant black holes that haven't eaten in millions of years—suddenly lighting up with a stolen meal.

climax.text: Surveys now detect several per year. Each one is a black hole revealing itself by destroying a passing star.

punchline.text: A star torn apart in real time. The black hole's location is revealed.

quiz.question: What is a tidal disruption event?
options: A black hole rips apart a star that passes too close, producing a bright flare
Two black holes collide and produce a massive energy burst
A star collapses into a black hole and emits a flash of light

details.summary: A tidal disruption event (TDE) occurs when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and is torn apart by tidal forces. Half the star's material spirals into the black hole in a superheated accretion flare, while the rest is flung away — producing a months-long burst of light across…
details.whyItMatters: TDEs provide rare glimpses of otherwise dormant supermassive black holes suddenly turning on. They reveal black hole properties, test tidal force predictions, and illuminate the environment near galactic centers.
takeaways: Stars torn apart by tidal forces near supermassive black holes
They produce bright flares lasting weeks to months
TDEs reveal properties of otherwise dormant black holes

faq.question: How often do tidal disruption events occur?
faq.answer: Roughly once every 10,000-100,000 years per galaxy. Since we can observe many galaxies, astronomers detect several dozen per year with modern surveys. The rate depends on stellar density near the galactic center and the black hole's mass and spin.

faq.question: Can any star be tidally disrupted?
faq.answer: If the black hole is too massive (above about 100 million solar masses for non-spinning holes), the star crosses the event horizon whole before tidal forces can tear it apart — there's no visible disruption. Spinning black holes can disrupt stars at somewhat higher masses.
